output.headline: Detectives’ tireless work leads to new terror charge in Widdecombe case
output.standfirst: A long-running counter-terrorism investigation has led to Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham, being charged with preparing terrorist acts, including a plot against Nigel Farage, after he was accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe.
output.bodyHtml:
A counter-terrorism investigation has led to a new charge against the man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe, with police saying he engaged in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism, including against Nigel Farage.

Counter-terrorism police said Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, relating to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year.

Vicki Evans, the head of counter-terrorism policing, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network.

“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”

Police said Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the charge raised “serious questions” about the security of MPs.

She wrote on X: “I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family.

“Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.

“This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve.”

A court previously heard that Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon.

Her gardener found her lying face down on her kitchen floor on the morning of 9 July, and emergency services declared her dead shortly afterwards.

Kerry is accused of her murder. At a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July, he spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address, and was not asked to indicate a plea.

Olivia Field, the chief executive of the Jo Cox Foundation, which was set up in honour of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016 in West Yorkshire, said: “No one in public life should have to fear for their safety.

“Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endanger individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life.

“We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics. That means looking across society – from education and political literacy to the safety of online environments – alongside ensuring that appropriate security and support are in place for politicians, their staff and families.”

Counter-terrorism police reopened a year-long investigation in August into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London.

The Metropolitan police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary” but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

After reopening the investigation, CTP London identified a line of inquiry that it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.
output.progress: Counter-terrorism police say a dedicated team of detectives, analysts and forensic experts led the investigation that resulted in the new charge.
